new_statements.quote: This chapter will examine some important features like vowel length and tone. Esimbi like many other African languages is a tone language, that is, a language in which both segmental and pitch phonemes, otherwise known as tones, go into the composition of words. In tone languages words can be distinguished on the basis of segments as well as on the basis of tones. [p. 73] ... There are basically five tones in Esimbi with three register and two contour tones. These tones are pertinent in the language [p. 74]
new_statements.citation: Fointein, Jacenta Nsang. 1986. Phonology of Esimbi. Maîtrise dissertation, University of Yaoundé. v+83 pp.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 5 'Suprasegmental phonology', p. 73 (PDF p. 79) and p. 74 (PDF p. 80)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (89 PDF pages, scanned layer, MPG PuRe scan of Fointein 1986 'Phonology of Esimbi', Univ. of Yaoundé maîtrise). Checked the quoted passage against the page images thesis p. 73) and thesis p. 74): both sentences are there word for word ('This chapter will examine some important features like vowel length and tone. Esimbi like many other African languages is a tone language, that is, a language in which both segmental and pitch phonemes, otherwise known as tones, go into the composition of words. In tone languages words can be distinguished on the basis of segments as well as on the basis of tones.' p. 73; 'There are basically five tones in Esimbi with three register and two contour tone…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Esimbi is described as a tone language with five lexical tones (high, mid, low, falling, rising); the only suprasegmental features treated are vowel length and tone. The thesis makes no statement about word stress or accent at all, so no stress position can be read from it.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: few minimal pairs by tone alone because words are multisyllabic; verbs (imperative) carry only H/L patterns (H or LH on monosyllables; HH/LH on disyllables; HHH/LLH/LHH on trisyllables); noun prefixes mostly L or H, exceptionally M/HL/LH.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical tone on words in isolation; verbs cited in imperative form). No phrase-level prosody discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Fointein 1986 describes Esimbi as spoken in the Benakuma area (Menchum Division, NW Cameroon); no dialect is singled out and the description is for the language as a whole (esim1238). Kalinowski 2009 likewise centres on Benakuma. No differently named variety is involved.

Chapter 5 'Suprasegmental phonology' (pp. 73-80) treats only vowel length and tone: Esimbi is called a tone language with five tones (H, M, L, HL falling, LH rising); the words 'stress', 'accent', 'prominence' do not occur anywhere in the scanned text and chapter 5 was read in full (page images pp. 73-74 checked).
Segment inventory only, sourced from Fointein 1986; no tones or stress listed.

sources.citation: Kalinowski, Cristin. 2009. Multidirectional vowel harmony in Esimbi. Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society 35(1): 146-154. DOI 10.3765/bls.v35i1.3606
sources.note: Nothing on stress; only a remark that homophonous imperatives are disambiguated by tone (p. 149). Cites Stallcup 1980, Hyman 1988, Walker 1999 (ms.) for Esimbi data.
Only orthographic note: acute = high tone, macron = mid tone; no stress statement. FR page bibliography lists Blench 2011 Tivoid wordlist, Fointein 1986, Kum 2017 primer.
